content: The scapula, commonly referred to as the shoulder blade, is a flat, triangular bone that connects the humerus (upper arm bone) to the clavicle (collarbone). It forms the posterior portion of the shoulder girdle and plays a critical role in the structure and function of the shoulder joint. Features of the Scapula: The scapula has two surfaces, three borders, and three angles. Anterior Surface (Costal Surface): The anterior surface of the scapula contains the subscapular fossa, a broad concavity where the subscapularis muscle attaches. The medial two-thirds of this fossa are marked by oblique ridges that provide attachment points for the tendinous insertions of the subscapularis muscle, while the lateral third is smooth and covered by the muscle fibers. The subscapular fossa is bordered by smooth triangular areas at the medial and inferior angles, which serve as attachment points for the serratus anterior muscle. A transverse depression near the upper part of the fossa, called the subscapular angle, strengthens the bone and supports the spine and acromion. Posterior Surface (Dorsal Surface): The posterior surface is divided by a prominent bony ridge called the spine of the scapula into two distinct regions: 1. Supraspinous Fossa: This smaller, concave area lies above the spine and is broader at its vertebral end. It provides the origin for the supraspinatus muscle. 2. Infraspinous Fossa: This larger area lies below the spine and features a shallow concavity near its vertebral margin, a central convexity, and a deep groove near the axillary border. The medial two-thirds of this fossa give origin to the infraspinatus muscle, while the lateral third is covered by the muscle. The dorsal surface also contains an elevated ridge near the axillary border, which serves as an attachment site for a fibrous septum separating the infraspinatus from the teres major and teres minor muscles. The lower third of this surface provides origin for the teres major muscle and serves as a gliding surface for the latissimus dorsi muscle, which may also originate from this region. Spine of the Scapula: The spine begins as a flat projection at the base of the scapula and ascends distally, reaching its peak at the tuber scapulae near the middle of the bone. Beyond this peak, the spine slopes downward and forward, forming the acromion, a hook-like structure that extends beyond the main body of the scapula. The acromion serves as an attachment site for muscles and forms the acromioclavicular joint with the clavicle. Coracoid Process: The coracoid process is another hook-like projection that arises from the lateral angle of the scapula. It serves as an attachment site for several muscles, including the coracobrachialis. Near its base lies the glenoid cavity, a depression that forms the socket for the head of the humerus, creating the glenohumeral joint. Borders of the Scapula: 1. Superior Border: The shortest and thinnest border, it is concave and extends from the medial angle to the base of the coracoid process. 2. Axillary Border (Lateral Border): The thickest border, it begins at the lower margin of the glenoid cavity and runs obliquely downward and backward to the inferior angle. 3. Vertebral Border (Medial Border): The longest border, it extends from the medial angle to the inferior angle. Angles of the Scapula: 1. Medial Angle (Superior Angle): Located at the uppermost part of the scapula. 2. Inferior Angle: The lowermost point of the scapula, where the medial and lateral borders meet. 3. Lateral Angle: The thickest part of the scapula, containing the glenoid cavity and the base of the coracoid process. Structure of the Scapula: The scapula is composed of cancellous (spongy) bone in its head, processes, and thickened regions, while the rest of the bone consists of a thin layer of compact bone. The central portions of the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae are often so thin that they may appear semitransparent. In some cases, the bone may be absent in these areas, leaving only fibrous tissue separating the adjacent muscles. Movements of the Scapula: The scapula is capable of several movements, which are facilitated by the surrounding muscles: Elevation: Lifting the scapula upward. Depression: Lowering the scapula downward. Protraction: Moving the scapula forward along the ribcage. Retraction: Pulling the scapula backward toward the spine. Lateral Rotation: Rotating the scapula outward, away from the midline. Medial Rotation: Rotating the scapula inward, toward the midline. The scapula's unique structure and articulation with the humerus and clavicle allow for a wide range of motion and functional versatility in the shoulder joint.
